German general Breuer elected to head top NATO military body

Reuters

19 September, 2026 09:30 pm IST

BRUSSELS, Sept 19 (Reuters) – General Carsten Breuer, Germany’s chief of defence, was chosen on Saturday as the next head of NATO’s military committee, the alliance’s top military authority and a key advisory body for its political leaders.

Military chiefs from the 32-nation alliance elected Breuer at a meeting in Copenhagen, current chair Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said in a post on X. Breuer will take up the role next summer, succeeding Dragone.

“Your operational judgement, your deep familiarity with this Alliance and your leadership of the German Armed Forces will serve NATO well,” Dragone wrote, congratulating Breuer.

Show Full Article

“The Chiefs of Defence have placed their trust in you at a demanding moment for Euro-Atlantic security,” he added.

The committee is NATO’s senior military authority and its chair serves as the main military adviser to its political chief, Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Breuer will assume the post at a time of upheaval in the alliance. US President Donald Trump has demanded that European countries take primary responsibility for the continent’s defence after decades of American leadership.

Many European governments have ramped up defence spending in recent years, driven both by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and by Trump’s threats not to honour US commitments to NATO.

Germany, Europe’s largest economy, has been at the forefront of the spending surge. Berlin aims to double its military expenditure to over €200 billion ($230 billion) by 2030.

Breuer, a 61-year-old army officer, earned the nickname “the chancellor’s general” after then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz picked him to lead a crisis committee that helped manage Germany’s response to the COVID pandemic in 2021 and 2022.

He joined the Bundeswehr in an air defence unit in 1984 and later attended the US general staff college in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, as well as German general staff training in Hamburg. In 2014, he served with NATO’s International Security Assistance Force in the Afghan capital Kabul.

Germany’s current army chief, Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, is expected to succeed Breuer as chief of defence before the end of the year.

($1 = 0.8709 euros)

(Reporting by Sabine Siebold and Lili Bayer. Editing by Andrew Gray)

Israeli strikes kill three people in Gaza, medics say

Reuters

19 September, 2026 08:30 pm IST

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

By Nidal al-Mughrabi CAIRO, Sept 19 (Reuters) – Israeli airstrikes killed at least three Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Saturday, health officials said.

One strike near Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza killed Basir Al-Bursh, the son of Munir Al-Bursh, the territory’s health ministry director-general, medics and family members said.

The Israeli military said it had struck several militants on Saturday, including Basir Al-Bursh, without giving further information. Hamas, the Palestinian militant group that runs Gaza, did not immediately comment.

Show Full Article

Munir Al-Bursh lost a daughter in an Israeli airstrike in December 2023, according to family members and medics. He was wounded in that attack.

In video obtained by Reuters, Al-Bursh was seen carrying his son’s body, wrapped in a blanket, with other mourners as it was rushed to hospital by ambulance.

“I was with him in the tent, and he said, Dad, they will target us, you and me together, I said that is fine, we will go to heaven together,” said Al-Bursh in the video.

“He went outside the tent and they struck him and he was martyred, may God have mercy on him,” added Al-Bursh.

At Al Shifa Hospital, Al-Bursh could barely stand as mourners arrived to pay their respects.

Elsewhere, a strike killed a man in Shejaia, east of Gaza City, while another hit a vehicle in the Sheikh Radwan district of Gaza City, killing one person, the civil defence service and medics said, taking Saturday’s death toll to at least three.

The Israeli military said the Sheikh Radwan strike targeted a Hamas militant. The blast reduced the vehicle to a mangled wreck.

Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.

A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory, but little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory’s health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.

(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi. Editing by Mark Potter)

Veto, sovereignty & military access—what US and Denmark could get out of Trump’s Greenland deal

Deal could be signed at UNGA next week, according to Danish leadership. Its signing could bring to an end saga between the US and the rest of NATO over the fate of the island.

Keshav Padmanabhan

19 September, 2026 06:51 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational | A drone view shows houses on the shore of Nuuk, Greenland, on 7 February, 2026 | Stoyan Nenov/Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US President Donald J. Trump’s Friday announcement, of an agreement with Denmark over Greenland, comes after months of high-stakes negotiations over an island that the American President has sought to purchase during the course of his two presidencies.

The announcement made by Trump is light on details of the full contours of the deal, but highlights key points of what Washington considers a part of the deal.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has welcomed the agreement as “great for NATO [North Atlantic Treaty Organisation] and Europe as well”.

Show Full Article

Trump’s deal for greater military access in Greenland falls short of his call for handing over the territory to the US, an outcome he had deemed as “unacceptable” in January. The new agreement, according to Trump, will ensure “permanent US control” over security of the self-governing autonomous territory part of the Kingdom of Denmark, while also underlining that “no adversary” will ever build a base on the island.

The agreement is likely to be signed next week on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), potentially easing transatlantic tensions.

Trump and the other NATO member-states, including Denmark, have had major differences over the fate of Greenland, especially as the US President called for either annexation or the purchase of the island during the early months of his second term.

ThePrint explains the contours of the deal as it currently stands.

Also Read: ‘Will not take Greenland by force…we will remember if Europe says no,’ Trump says at Davos

‘Permanent control’ over security of Greenland The agreement is expected to allow greater American military presence in Greenland, while preventing China or Russia from stationing troops or building bases in the strategically placed Arctic island, according to Bloomberg .

The US will be empowered to restrict investments in Greenland made by countries it deems as adversaries, reports Bloomberg , while also allowing Washington to act to safeguard its interests in the region.

The island found to the Northeast of Canada is roughly 2.16 million square kilometres in size, with over 39,000 kilometres of coastline. Around 80 percent of the island is covered by a large ice-sheet, which is the second largest in the world, following Antarctica.

The strategic importance of Greenland has grown in recent decades, especially with record rates of melting ice across the Arctic, which has led to more activities by countries in the region.

Russia is one of the eight countries to have a geographical footprint in the Arctic, alongside Canada, Norway, Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Sweden and the US.

Other countries including China and India have also shown interest in the Arctic for multiple reasons. From research into the melting ice-caps for better understanding of glacial melt in the Himalayas, to the Northern Sea Route, the region has increasingly become important for countries outside its immediate vicinity.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many. We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction,” Trump said in a statement on the micro-blogging platform X.

The latest agreement could potentially allow the US a potential veto over any investments in Greenland from countries like Russia and China, given American concerns that Chinese or Russian investment, especially in sensitive areas such as minerals, could impact the US’ position in Greenland.

The US in Greenland since WWII The US’ interest in Greenland is not new. Since World War II, its military has had a presence in Greenland. The American military moved quickly to capture the island during WWII, after NAZI Germany occupied Denmark in the summer of 1940.

Denmark and the US eventually negotiated a military treaty in 1951, which allowed the US the right to build military bases across Greenland as long as prior consent was sought from Copenhagen.

The US will likely not require any consent from Denmark or Greenland to expand its military footprint on the island, according to the BBC . Throughout the Cold War, the US maintained a number of military installations in Greenland, especially as the polar route was the quickest trajectory for an inter-continental ballistic missile between the US and the Soviet Union.

The US eventually reduced the number of its active bases to just one at Thule, which was renamed as the Pituffik Space Base in 2023. The US-Denmark 1951 agreement has been amended and supplemented in the past, including in 2004 signed in Igaliku between the two countries. The primary fixture in all these agreements remained the Danish consent required for US military presence.

The agreement, which could be signed next week on the margins of the UNGA, may finally bring to an end the ongoing chapter between the US and the rest of NATO over the fate of Greenland. Trump’s provocative claims, including over the territory, had led to an united response by Europe, which inflamed tensions within the transatlantic partnership.

Frederiksen’s response to the agreement highlights that the deal recognises Denmark’s sovereignty over the Arctic island. Greenland also welcomed the agreement, while making no comment on the final contours of the deal.

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)
